summary: Reports on an Internet Architecture Board workshop in October 2006 in Amsterdam on routing and addressing. Its aim was a shared understanding of the routing scalability problems that large backbone operators face. Findings cover what drives routing table growth, router technology limits, and limits of the addressing architecture.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4984 reports what network operators and router vendors discussed at an IAB routing and addressing workshop. The report identifies why global routing tables were growing and what a future solution would need to consider.

tldr.problem: Large backbone operators reported growing routing tables, more routing updates, and increasing costs for high-performance routers.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB held a workshop in Amsterdam and reported its participants' findings, including the causes of route growth and criteria for evaluating solutions.
tldr.outcome: The report identifies routing scalability and the use of IP addresses as both identifiers and locators as top concerns. It records workshop participants' views, not an official IAB position.

sections.title: A Workshop Report, Not an IAB Position
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board held its Routing and Addressing Workshop in Amsterdam on October 18-19, 2006. Its goal was to develop a shared understanding of routing scalability problems faced by large backbone operators and provide input for later work.

The RFC reports the workshop proceedings. Its views and priorities belong to the participants, who were mostly large network operators and some router vendors, rather than to the IAB as an institution.
sections.plainLanguage: This document records a workshop about routing and addressing. It presents the participants' conclusions, not an official IAB position.

sections.title: The Main Routing and Addressing Problems
sections.content:
Participants ranked routing-system scalability as the highest-priority problem. They discussed growth in the Default Free Zone routing and forwarding tables, the work needed to recompute forwarding information, BGP convergence, and the cost and power of core router hardware.

The second major problem was that an IP address serves both as a locator, which helps routing find a network, and an identifier, which names an endpoint. Participants said that this overload makes it difficult to keep addresses aligned with network topology and that a locator-identifier split seemed necessary, although the workshop did not design one.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop identified two main issues: routing information was growing, and IP addresses were serving two different roles. The report does not specify a solution to either problem.

sections.title: What Drives Route Growth
sections.content:
The report identifies multihoming, traffic engineering, address allocations that cannot be aggregated, and business events such as mergers as drivers of routing-table growth. These factors can lead operators to advertise more-specific prefixes, increasing both the table and the number of BGP updates.

Customers may seek provider-independent addresses to avoid renumbering or to connect through more than one provider. Traffic engineering can also require more-specific route advertisements. The report notes that the party receiving a benefit from an added route may not bear the system-wide cost of carrying it.
sections.plainLanguage: More-specific routes help individual networks manage connections and traffic. Each route also adds information that routers throughout the system may need to process.

sections.title: Router Technology and Scaling Costs
sections.content:
The report challenges the assumption that Moore's Law will automatically keep router costs in line with routing-table growth. Core routers use specialized components produced in much lower volumes than general-purpose processors, so the report says those components do not receive the same cost advantages.

It discusses DRAM access speed, off-chip SRAM, chip-development costs, heat, and power as constraints. Its summary estimates sustainable table growth of 1.3 times per two years for forwarding tables and 1.2 times per two years for routing tables, while noting that the hardware discussion had generated debate and needed further community input.
sections.plainLanguage: Router hardware does not necessarily get cheaper fast enough to match routing-table growth. Memory speed, specialized chips, heat, and power all constrain how routers scale.

sections.title: Solution Criteria and Workshop Recommendations
sections.content:
The report reviews earlier approaches, including SHIM6, GSE, and Map-and-Encap, and describes tradeoffs in host changes, mapping services, and provider control. It lists evaluation criteria: scale in global and internal routes, support traffic engineering, provide incentives for lower system cost, work incrementally, and account for IPv4 and IPv6.

Workshop participants recommended starting long-term work, consulting other stakeholders, involving the research community, considering interim measures such as FIB compression, and creating a roadmap. They said security should be considered early, while noting that securing the routing system was not itself a requirement for solution development.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop recommended open work with a roadmap and input from more groups. Any solution would need to scale while supporting gradual deployment and traffic engineering.
